svg.aria-label: A lumbar vertebra seen from above: the load bearing body lies in front, the arch of pedicles, laminae and spinous process encloses the vertebral foramen behind it, and of all these parts only the spinous process can be felt through the skin.

g.text: anterior at the top, posterior at the bottom

g.data-tip: The thick block of bone at the front that carries almost all of the load passed down the column. Its flat top and bottom surfaces are where the intervertebral discs attach. It sits deep inside the trunk and cannot be reached from the back.

The opening enclosed by the body in front and the arch behind. Stacked one on another these openings form the vertebral canal. In the lumbar region the canal holds the cauda equina rather than the spinal cord itself, because the cord usually ends near L1 or L2.

The short thick strut that joins the arch to the body, and the strongest part of the arch. Notches on its upper and lower edges form the roof and the floor of the intervertebral foramen, so the pedicles set the height of the opening each spinal nerve leaves through.

A long thin lever sticking out sideways for muscles and ligaments to pull on. In the lumbar region it lies buried under the erector spinae mass, so it is felt only indirectly and never as clearly as the spinous process.

The flat plate that roofs the vertebral canal from behind. It is the piece of bone removed in a laminectomy, and it is the broad surface a practitioner contacts when a thrust is not delivered on the spinous process itself.

The upward facing pillar that meets the downward facing process of the vertebra above to form a facet joint. Two of these joints and one disc make up the three joint complex of a single motion segment.

The cartilage covered joint surface itself. Its plane decides which movements the segment allows. In the lumbar spine it lies close to the sagittal plane and faces backward and inward, which is why this region bends forward freely and rotates very little.

A small tubercle on the back of the superior articular process. The multifidus and a slip of longissimus attach here. It is a target used on imaging rather than something a hand can find through the muscle.

The narrow bridge of bone between the superior and the inferior articular process. It carries the load that passes from one facet joint to the next and it is the usual site of the stress fracture called spondylolysis, most often at L5 in young athletes.

The blade of bone projecting straight backward in the midline. This is the part you can feel through the skin, and for most examiners it is the only part of the vertebra they ever touch, which is why so much of spinal examination rests on one small bony tip.
